source.title: Computed Gotos in C (Direct Threaded Code)

cards.question: What GNU C extension syntax is used to take the address of a label and jump to it dynamically?
cards.answer: The unary && operator takes the label address (e.g. &&op_add), and goto *pointer; performs the indirect jump.

cards.question: Why does a traditional interpreter loop using while (running) { switch (fetch()) { ... } } suffer from CPU branch mispredictions?
cards.answer: All instructions jump back to the same central switch header, forcing the CPU branch predictor to predict an ever-changing target from a single branch site, causing pipeline stalls.

cards.question: How does Direct Threaded Code using computed gotos eliminate the central interpreter loop bottleneck?
cards.answer: Each instruction handler dispatches directly to the next handler by fetching the opcode and jumping through a dispatch table (goto *dispatch_table[fetch()]), decentralizing branch prediction across distinct jump sites.

cards.question: Why can computed gotos execute faster than a compiler-optimized jump table generated for a switch statement?
cards.answer: A switch statement must generate default bounds-checking instructions to satisfy the ISO standard, whereas computed gotos skip bounds checks and provide separate branch prediction state per opcode.

cards.question: What are the main engineering trade-offs of using computed gotos in a C project?
cards.answer: They are non-standard compiler extensions unsupported by MSVC, make step-through debugging more complex, and require dispatch macro duplication across all handlers.
